quirks: Civil registration began 1 July 1837 at the England and Wales national level (Wolverhampton Registration District). Compliance was imperfect until 1874 when penalties were introduced — a birth c.1857 should be registered but may be missing; check adjacent quarters and adjacent districts (Penkridge, Walsall) if not found in Wolverhampton.

A christening date in a church register is the date of baptism, not the date of birth. Victorian Anglican practice often baptised children months or years after birth. The baptism register entry for 30 January 1868 must be viewed directly to read any stated birth date or age for the child.

The ancient parish of Wolverhampton St Peter (registers from 1603; Bishop's Transcripts from 1799) subdivided into at least ten daughter ecclesiastical parishes between 1832 and 1849. For events in 1850-1910, the correct parish register depends on which neighbourhood the family lived in — identify the address from a census return first.

Wolverhampton had active Nonconformist congregations (Wesleyan, Baptist, Independent, Presbyterian, Unitarian). Post-1837 Nonconformist baptism registers are not in the FamilySearch Staffordshire Church Records collection (CoE only); they are held by individual congregations or denominational archives.

Pre-1846 probate for Wolverhampton fell under the Court of the Peculiar of Wolverhampton; 1846-1858 under the Bishop of Lichfield's Consistory Court; from 1858 under the Principal Probate Registry (national). An index of wills at Wolverhampton Archives is downloadable at wolverhamptonhistory.org.uk.

The GRO's own free online birth index (gro.gov.uk) includes the mother's maiden name — a significant advantage over FreeBMD for distinguishing multiple children of the same name in the Wolverhampton district.
Surname spelling was unstandardised; search phonetic variants of Earnest (Ernest, Arnest) and Grice (Gryce) in all indexes.

The re-use of a given name within the same family almost always indicates the earlier child of that name died — a second 'Hannah' in a family register is evidence of infant death, not a duplicate record.
The 1891 census surname/folio index for the Wolverhampton district (including Bilston, Tettenhall, Wednesfield, Willenhall, Wombourn) compiled by BMSGH is at FamilySearch Library on film 6393534.
Civil registration events are filed by the date registered, not the date of the event. A birth in late December registered in January will appear in the following year's Q1 index.

Question: q_001 — "When was Hannah Earnest born, and does the 30 January 1868 Christening record at Wolverhampton belong to her or to another individual?"

Key context:
- Hannah Earnest (tree id: 9DJ7-219) has a birth year of ~1857 in the tree, but also carries a Christening dated 30 Jan 1868 at Wolverhampton
- A Residence entry places her in 1861, before the 1868 christening date — but note that Victorian christenings often occurred long after birth, so the 1868 christening and an 1857 birth are NOT necessarily contradictory; the conflict only stands if the baptism entry explicitly records an age or birth date inconsistent with 1857
- Parents: Joseph Ernest (2DXV-X2R) and Diana Haines (MCVR-HGZ)
- Husband: Edwin Grice (9DJ7-2BY), children include John, Hannah Grace, Edwin, William, James
- Locality guide persisted as loc_001 for Wolverhampton/Staffordshire, England, 1850–1910

Please create a sequenced research plan for q_001, targeting:
1. England & Wales civil registration birth index (GRO) for Hannah Earnest, Wolverhampton district, ~1855–1870
2. FamilySearch England census records (1861, 1871) to find Hannah in her parents' household and establish her age
3. Staffordshire/Wolverhampton baptism registers for the 30 Jan 1868 christening entry, to read the stated birth date/age
4. Any additional record sets that would resolve her birth year and the christening attribution

After q_001 is resolved, the plan should include steps toward the main completeness question about additional Grice children.

entry.rationale: The tree records Hannah's birth year as 1857 in Darlaston but no GRO registration entry has been found or cited. The England and Wales, Birth Registration Index, 1837-2008 (name-searchable) covers this district and period and is the first source to check. Civil registration began 1 July 1837; compliance improved after 1874, so a birth c.1857 should exist but may be filed under a phonetic variant (Arnest, Ernest). The GRO birth index also includes the mother's maiden name from 1837 onwards, which will confirm parentage. Search phonetic variants of Earnest (Ernest, Arnest) and expand to adjacent districts (Walsall, Penkridge) if not found in Wolverhampton. The result will show the registered birth year, the exact quarter, and the district — supplying the anchor date that all other items depend on.

Fallback for the FamilySearch birth index search. Ancestry hosts the England and Wales, Civil Registration Birth Index, 1837-1915 (name-searchable), drawn from the same GRO source. If the FamilySearch index returns nothing under Earnest/Ernest/Arnest across the Wolverhampton and adjacent districts, Ancestry's version should be tried with the same phonetic variants, as the two indexes have been transcribed independently and may carry different errors. The GRO's own free online birth index at gro.gov.uk (includes mother's maiden name) is a further check if both index searches fail.

The tree already records Hannah's 1861 Residence at Darlaston and cites source 9F5F-VZ7 (England and Wales, Census, 1861, entry for Joseph Earnest and Diana Earnest). That source has been attached but not yet extracted: the census image must be read to record the age stated for Hannah in April 1861, which is the earliest documentary age evidence predating the 1868 christening. If the 1861 return gives her age as approximately 3-4 she was born c.1857-58, consistent with the tree; if it gives 1-2 she was born c.1859-60, which would put the 1868 christening only eight or nine years after birth — still plausible for Victorian delayed baptism, but narrowing the window. The England and Wales, Census, 1861 collection is name-searchable. The 1861 census is the dependency that sets the outer birth-year boundary for the GRO search.

The tree records Hannah's 1871 Residence at Wolverhampton and cites source 9V1G-YQQ (England and Wales, Census, 1871, entry for Joseph Hirnist and Dianah Hirnist — note the heavy phonetic distortion of the surname Earnest/Ernest to Hirnist). That source is attached but not yet extracted. Reading the 1871 household image gives Hannah's stated age in April 1871, providing a second independent age witness. Combined with the 1861 age, the two censuses bracket her birth year. The 1871 entry also locates the family in Wolverhampton, confirming the geographic context for the January 1868 christening at St John Wolverhampton. The England and Wales, Census, 1871 collection is name-searchable. Note the variant spelling; search as Hirnist and Ernest.

The tree carries two overlapping fact entries for the 30 January 1868 event: a Baptism at Wolverhampton and a Christening at St John, Wolverhampton, both citing source SWZ4-P1R (England, Staffordshire, Church Records, 1538-1944). That source has been attached but not yet extracted. The image of the actual register entry must be read to answer the core question: does the entry state a birth date or age for the child, and is the child's father named as Joseph Ernest/Earnest? The Staffordshire Church Records collection (id 2364451) is name-searchable. Victorian Anglican baptism registers in this period used the standard register format that recorded the child's birth date in a separate column from the baptism date — reading that column resolves whether the stated birth date is consistent with 1857 or contradicts it. The loc_001 quirk notes that St Peter's (the ancient mother church) subdivided into daughter parishes by 1849; St John is one of those daughters, so the search must be scoped to that specific parish.

Fallback for item 5. FindMyPast hosts Staffordshire Baptisms, 1538-1900 (name-searchable), a separate transcription of the same Staffordshire parish register series. If the FamilySearch Staffordshire Church Records index does not surface the 30 January 1868 entry or does not link to the register image, the FindMyPast version may carry a different transcription or link to the image via a different route. Also consider FreeReg (freereg.org.uk) as a no-cost alternative transcription for the same parish. The loc_001 quirk notes that Nonconformist baptism registers are not in the CoE FamilySearch collection; if the family is identified as Nonconformist (Diana Haines was baptised Wesleyan at Wednesbury in 1828), check the England and Wales, Non-Conformist Record Indexes (RG4-8), 1588-1977 on FamilySearch, though this collection covers pre-1837 registered congregations and may not hold post-1837 Wesleyan records.

The tree records a 1881 Residence for Hannah at West Bromwich (not Wolverhampton) and cites source QYLW-S5N (England and Wales, Census, 1881, entry for Edwin Grice and Hannah Grice). That source is attached but not yet extracted. Reading the 1881 census image gives Hannah's stated age as wife of Edwin Grice, providing a third independent age witness — triangulating between the 1861 and 1871 census ages. It also establishes the number and ages of children present in 1881, which is directly relevant to the project's main objective of identifying additional Grice children (a child absent from the 1881 household but present in 1871 or 1891 would be a candidate for an unrecorded death or a mis-attributed record). The England and Wales, Census, 1881 collection is name-searchable.

The tree records a 1891 Residence for Hannah at Birmingham and cites source 7BL6-KLH (England and Wales, Census, 1891, entry for Edwin Grice and Hannah Grice). That source is attached but not yet extracted. Reading the 1891 census image gives Hannah's stated age as a fourth and later-life age witness, and — crucially for the project objective — establishes the full list of children living in the household in 1891. Any Grice child appearing in 1881 but absent in 1891 (with no death record traced) or any child appearing in 1891 not in the current tree is an answer to the completeness question. The loc_001 quirk notes the BMSGH 1891 Wolverhampton district index on film 6393534 covers Bilston, Tettenhall, Wednesfield, Willenhall and Wombourn — but the family had moved to Birmingham by 1891 so the Warwickshire census applies. The England and Wales, Census, 1891 collection is name-searchable.

FAN item required for an identity and completeness question. The known Grice children span 1877-1886 (John, Hannah Grace, Edwin, William, James). The England and Wales, Birth Registration Index, 1837-2008 (name-searchable) should be searched for all births registered to Grice in the Wolverhampton, Walsall, and West Bromwich districts between 1876 and approximately 1895, to test whether additional children were registered but are absent from the tree. A re-used given name within the family (per the loc_001 quirk) signals an earlier child of that name died; comparing the GRO index against the five known children may surface unregistered siblings. The date window is sized to span the parents' plausible fertility period: Hannah born c.1857 and Edwin born c.1854, so children from c.1876 to c.1895 are realistic. This item is a prerequisite to the project objective and feeds directly into the main completeness question.

Companion FAN item: search the England and Wales, Death Registration Index 1837-2007 (name-searchable) for deaths of children surnamed Grice in the West Bromwich, Wolverhampton, and Birmingham districts between 1876 and 1895. The loc_001 quirk on re-used given names means a second child named 'Hannah' in the family would indicate the first Hannah Grace died; a death-index search for infant Grices in this period will either confirm known deaths or surface unrecorded ones. A child born and registered in item 9's search but not traceable in any later census would have a death entry here. This item is bounded by the parents' residential history (West Bromwich from c.1877, Birmingham from c.1891) and the oldest known child's birth year (1877).

guardrail_shadow_violations.detail: person_evidence link written for new tree person(s) I1 with no prior same_person call: a brand-new identity should be scored before it is asserted (person-evidence/SKILL.md doctrine; issue #963). Score them with the project-relative form, which assembles both documents for you: `same_person({ projectPath, assertionId, treePersonId: "I1" })`. `assertionId` is the assertion the link cites. The tool resolves the record itself and builds the tree side as that person's matching mob, so you hand-build nothing (person-evidence, 'Call it with references, not documents'). If this call was denied, the entire batch was rejected — including any ops in other sections — and must be re-issued after the same_person call. A relationship or marriage assertion names two parties and gets a link for each. The call is about the assertion's own `record_role` party by default; for the OTHER party add `recordRole` (or `recordPersonaId`) naming it. Reusing the first party's persona for the second is how a near-zero score gets manufactured and then explained away. If the tool answers that the record holds no persona for that party, or that the candidate is a stub minted from the very persona you would be scoring (circular), say so in the link's `rationale` and proceed — the gap is still recorded; the rationale is the record of why, not a waiver. How the assertion was RETRIEVED is not such a case: a full-text hit, an image, a PDF and a sidecar-less search are all scorable, because the tool derives the record side from the record's own assertions when it cannot fetch a document. A locally-minted tree id is NOT such a case: it scores on document content and must be scored.
